tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. - Reads up to 2000 lines by default.

tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

# lumen

A from-scratch JavaScript **engine** in Rust — std only, zero dependencies — and a
**runtime** being built on top of it, the way Node/Deno/Bun wrap a JS engine with an event
loop and host APIs. Every crate in the workspace is std-only: no `tokio`, `mio`, `libc`,
`rustyline`, `serde`, or any other third-party dependency, anywhere.

## The engine (`crates/lumen`)

A lexer, parser, and **three execution tiers**:

- a **tree-walking interpreter** — the reference oracle: the spec semantics live here, and
  every other tier must match it observably (a differential fuzzer, `lumen-difftest`, holds
  them to that);
- an opt-in **bytecode VM** — functions compile whole (or not at all — no deoptimization) to
  a stack machine with slot-homed locals, per-site inline caches for property and free-name
  access backed by object shapes (hidden classes), and dense-array element fast paths;
- a **native template JIT** — bytecode lowers to real ARM64 machine code on macOS, Linux,
  and Windows, with a correctness-first x86-64 backend on Intel macOS, Linux, and Windows:
  per-op templates with the interpreter as the shared slow path, inline-cache reads baked
  into the instruction stream, fused compare-and-branch, exact-`ToInt32` bitops, and numeric
  *register chains* that keep runs of arithmetic entirely in FP registers. The full set of
  inline fast paths currently lives in the ARM64 backend; x86-64 starts with native control
  flow and checked per-op helpers. Other architectures degrade to the bytecode VM.

Tier selection: `--tier=interp|bytecode|jit` (**jit is the default**; where the JIT is
unavailable it degrades to the bytecode VM). Functions tier up after a call-count threshold —
immediately if the body contains a loop. Force the reference tree-walker with `--tier=interp`
(or `LUMEN_TIER=interp`).

The language surface: generators and `async`/`await` running on stackful coroutines (async
bodies suspend on the bytecode VM itself), full `RegExp` (including `\p{…}` and inline
modifiers), typed arrays, `Proxy`/`Reflect`, ES modules (top-level await, `import defer`,
source phase), `Intl`, and `Temporal`.

`Intl` (ECMA-402) and `Temporal` are behind the default-on `intl` and `temporal` Cargo features.
The CLDR data tables included by `intl` are the largest single contributor to binary size (~3 MB
of the release binary). Build with `--no-default-features` for a small engine: the `Intl` and
`Temporal` globals are absent, `Date.prototype.toTemporalInstant` is omitted, and the `toLocale*`
methods degrade to their locale-independent forms, the way engines built without i18n do. Either
feature can be enabled independently.

On dependencies and `unsafe`: the workspace stays std-only — the JIT maps executable memory
through raw platform declarations (`mmap`/`mprotect`, macOS `MAP_JIT`, or Windows
`VirtualAlloc`/`VirtualProtect`) rather than libc. Pages are writable only while code is copied,
then executable/read-only, and instruction caches are synchronized where required. The
interpreter and bytecode VM are safe Rust; `unsafe` is concentrated where machine
code meets the object graph (the JIT's executable pages and its templates' raw reads — every
baked offset is *measured at runtime* against the live types and fails closed to the checked
helper if anything doesn't hold) and in the N-API addon loader's `dlopen` bridge.

**Passes 100% of [tc39/test262](https://github.com/tc39/test262): 53,400/53,400** (including
annexB, intl402, and staging) — on the default JIT tier and under `LUMEN_TIER=interp`.

Extracted from — and used by — the [lucid-softworks/browser](https://github.com/lucid-softworks/browser)
engine as its JS backend (`backend-lumen`), with full git history.

## The runtime

A curated `embed` API on the engine exposes just enough — native-function registration, a
typed host-state slot, and event-loop hooks — for a runtime layer to be assembled from
independent op crates, without leaking the interpreter's internals into the published API.
On top of that:

- **Event loop** (`lumen-runtime`) — a single loop thread owns the (`!Send`) engine; blocking
  work runs on a std thread pool and completes back over `mpsc`. No epoll/kqueue reactor
  (that would need raw syscalls); the thread-pool-plus-completion model is libuv's own fs
  strategy. Each turn drains microtasks, queued callbacks, due timers, and I/O completions,
  then blocks until the next event.
- **Timers** (`lumen-timers`) — `setTimeout`/`setInterval`/`clearTimeout`/`clearInterval`/
  `setImmediate`, plus `queueMicrotask`.
- **`console` and `process`** — streaming `console.*`; `process.argv`/`env`/`platform`/
  `cwd()`/`exit()`/`nextTick()`.
- **Filesystem** (`lumen-fs`) — synchronous ops (`readFileSync`, `writeFileSync`,
  `existsSync`, `mkdirSync`, `readdirSync`, …), file handles via a resource table
  (`openSync`/`readSync`/`writeSync`/`closeSync`), and async `fs.promises.readFile`/
  `writeFile` on the thread pool.
- **Web platform** (`lumen-web`) — a growing slice of the WinterTC Minimum Common API:
  `Event`/`EventTarget`/`CustomEvent`/`AbortController`/`AbortSignal`/`DOMException`,
  `TextEncoder`/`TextDecoder`, `atob`/`btoa`, `structuredClone`, `URL`/`URLSearchParams`,
  `performance.now()`, `crypto.getRandomValues`/`randomUUID`/`subtle.digest` (SHA-256), and
  `fetch`/`Headers`/`Request`/`Response`. See the checklist at the top of
  `crates/lumen-web/src/lib.rs` for what's implemented vs. deferred (streams, `Blob`/
  `FormData`, `URLPattern`, …).

  `fetch` speaks HTTP/1.1 over `std::net`. **`https:` is not supported**: TLS cannot be
  implemented on std alone and no third-party crate is permitted, so `https` URLs reject with
  a clear error; plain `http` works.

  `Lumen.serve((request) => Response)` is the matching HTTP/1.1 **server** — not a WinterTC API,
  but the cross-runtime `serve(handler)` convention (Deno/Bun/Workers), so a Hono app runs with
  `Lumen.serve(app.fetch)`. v1 is single-accept, `Connection: close`, buffered bodies, http only
  (see `crates/lumen-web/src/server.rs`). Cold-start and usage: `examples/hono-app`.

- **Modules — both CommonJS and ESM.** `lumen-cli` picks the module kind the way Node does:
  `.mjs` is ESM, `.cjs` is CommonJS, `.js` follows the nearest `package.json` `"type"`. ES
  modules run through the engine's real module graph (linking, top-level `await`); `import`
  specifiers resolve against disk and `node_modules`, `node:` builtins are importable
  (named imports included), and CommonJS packages interop by default export. CommonJS files
  run as the program entry with `require.main === module`.

- **`node:` compatibility** (`lumen-node`) — a CommonJS `require` with `node_modules`
  resolution and the module wrapper, `package.json` `main`/`exports`, the `node:path`/
  `node:os`/`node:fs` builtins, and `Buffer`, so packages written against the `node:` surface
  run. See the checklist at the top of `crates/lumen-node/src/lib.rs` for the deferred pieces
  (subpath-pattern exports, the full N-API surface).

  **Native addons** load too: `require('./addon.node')` dlopens the compiled library and runs its
  N-API registration, resolving the addon's `napi_*` symbols against the lumen executable — the
  same mechanism the `node` binary uses. The N-API surface is implemented from scratch (values,
  properties, functions, callbacks, errors, references, object wrap, classes, promises, buffers,
  typed arrays, async work); the loader reaches `dlopen`/`dlsym` through raw `extern "C"`
  declarations, so no third-party crate is added. See `examples/native-addon`.

  **`vite build` runs on lumen** (`examples/vite-app`): a full Vite production build, bundling
  through Rollup's native N-API addon, transforming with esbuild's service subprocess, over
  ESM↔CommonJS interop and the `node:` surface — building `dist/` and exiting cleanly.

- **REPL + CLI** (`lumen-repl`, `lumen-cli`) — an interactive shell with a persistent realm,
  parser-driven incomplete-input detection (multi-line continuation), top-level `await`, and
  loop-to-quiescence so timers and awaited promises settle before the next prompt. Line
  editing is line-buffered (raw-mode/history would need `termios`); use `rlwrap` for arrows
  and history.

### Workspace crates

```
lumen          engine (std-only, zero-dep; `embed` feature gates the runtime API)
lumen-host     substrate: OpState, ResourceTable, Extension, the thread-pool/callback primitives
lumen-timers   setTimeout/setInterval/queueMicrotask/setImmediate
lumen-fs       filesystem (sync + async)
lumen-web      WinterTC Minimum Common API (Event, URL, crypto, fetch, …)
lumen-node     node: compatibility (require, node:path/os/fs, Buffer)
lumen-runtime  the event loop; assembles the op crates; console + process
lumen-repl     interactive shell
lumen-cli      node/deno-style entrypoint

test262-runner   conformance harness (parallel workers over ./test262)
lumen-difftest   differential fuzzer across the three execution tiers
lumen-wasm       wasm build of the engine
```

The dependency graph is a strict DAG — `lumen ← lumen-host ← {op crates} ← lumen-runtime ←
lumen-repl ← lumen-cli` — so each op crate can be worked on in isolation.

## Install

Grab a nightly prebuilt runtime on macOS arm64/x86_64 or Linux x86_64/arm64 (tagged releases
also publish Windows x86_64 binaries):

```sh
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lucid-softworks/lumen/main/scripts/install.sh | bash
```

It installs the `lumen` CLI to `~/.lumen/bin` from the rolling `nightly` release
(`LUMEN_INSTALL` and `LUMEN_RELEASE` override the location and tag). Other platforms build from
source — see below.

## Usage

Run scripts / open a REPL through the runtime:

```sh
cargo build --release -p lumen-cli
./target/release/lumen-cli                 # REPL (or: lumen-cli repl)
./target/release/lumen-cli file.js [args]  # run a script to loop quiescence
./target/release/lumen-cli -e 'code'       # evaluate a string
```

The engine also ships a minimal standalone shell (the test262 host, no runtime/host APIs):

```sh
cargo build --release -p lumen --bin lumen
./target/release/lumen file.js [more.js ...]
```

## Conformance

```sh
scripts/test262-clone.sh    # one-time: clone the suite into ./test262
scripts/run-test262.sh      # run it (see crates/test262-runner for env knobs)
LUMEN_TIER=jit scripts/run-test262.sh    # same suite against the compiled tiers
```

The execution tiers are also held together by a differential fuzzer: every generated program
runs in all three tiers, which must agree on the completion value, thrown errors, the
observable side-effect trace, and final global state. Divergences are delta-minimized into a
regression corpus that replays on every run.

```sh
cargo run --release -p lumen-difftest -- --count 2000
```

import heapq
def huff_heap(freqs, tiebreak='index'):
    """Classic heap Huffman. freqs: dict sym->count (count>0). Returns sym->len."""
    items = [(c, i, (s,)) for i, (s, c) in enumerate(sorted(freqs.items()))]
    if len(items) == 1:
        return {items[0][2][0]: 1}
    heapq.heapify(items)
    cnt = len(items)
    depth = {s: 0 for s in freqs}
    while len(items) > 1:
        c1, i1, s1 = heapq.heappop(items)
        c2, i2, s2 = heapq.heappop(items)
        for s in s1 + s2: depth[s] += 1
        heapq.heappush(items, (c1 + c2, cnt, s1 + s2)); cnt += 1
    return depth
def brotli_ref(freqs_arr, limit=15):
    """Brotli reference BrotliCreateHuffmanTree."""
    length = len(freqs_arr)
    count_limit = 1
    while True:
        tree = []
        for i in range(length - 1, -1, -1):
            if freqs_arr[i]:
                count = max(freqs_arr[i], count_limit)
                tree.append([count, -1, i])
        n = len(tree)
        if n == 1:
            return {tree[0][2]: 1}
        # stable sort by count ascending (SortHuffmanTreeItems with comparator total_count_ < ; ties: index_right_or_value_ larger first?)
        tree.sort(key=lambda t: (t[0], -t[2] if False else 0))
        # brotli comparator: if counts equal, compare index_right_or_value_ (b->index > a->index)
        tree.sort(key=lambda t: (t[0], -t[2]))
        sentinel = [1 << 30, -1, -1]
        nodes = [[t[0], -1, t[2], None, None] for t in tree]
        # use the two-queue algorithm
        # build in a list: leaves 0..n-1, then sentinel, then internal nodes
        arr = [[t[0], -1, t[2]] for t in tree] + [[1<<30, -1, -1], [1<<30, -1, -1]]
        i = 0; j = n + 1
        for k in range(n - 1, 0, -1):
            if arr[i][0] <= arr[j][0]: left = i; i += 1
            else: left = j; j += 1
            if arr[i][0] <= arr[j][0]: right = i; i += 1
            else: right = j; j += 1
            jend = 2 * n - k
            arr[jend] = [arr[left][0] + arr[right][0], left, right]
            arr.append([1 << 30, -1, -1])
        depth = {}
        def walk(p, lvl):
            if arr[p][1] >= 0:
                walk(arr[p][1], lvl + 1); walk(arr[p][2], lvl + 1)
            else:
                depth[arr[p][2]] = lvl
        walk(2 * n - 1, 0)
        if max(depth.values()) <= limit:
            return depth
        count_limit *= 2

def heap_general(hist, leaf_key, int_key):
    """leaf_key(sym, idx) -> tuple secondary key; int_key(nxt, a, b) -> secondary key."""
    syms = sorted(hist)
    if len(syms) == 1: return {syms[0]: 1}
    heap = []
    for i, s in enumerate(syms):
        heap.append(((hist[s],) + leaf_key(s, i), (s,)))
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    depth = {s: 0 for s in syms}
    nxt = 0
    while len(heap) > 1:

        kb, b = heapq.heappop(heap)
        for s in a + b: depth[s] += 1
        nxt += 1
        heapq.heappush(heap, ((ka[0] + kb[0],) + int_key(nxt, ka, kb), a + b))

def heap_general2(items, int_key):

def package_merge(hist, L):
    syms = sorted(hist, key=lambda s: (hist[s], s))
    n = len(syms)
    # standard package-merge: lists of (weight, multiset of symbols)
    leaves = [(hist[s], [s]) for s in syms]
    cur = list(leaves)
    for _ in range(L - 1):
        pk = []
        for i in range(0, len(cur) - 1, 2):
            pk.append((cur[i][0] + cur[i+1][0], cur[i][1] + cur[i+1][1]))
        cur = sorted(leaves + pk, key=lambda x: x[0])
    sel = cur[:2 * n - 2]
    d = collections.Counter()
    for w, ss in sel:
        for s in ss: d[s] += 1
    return dict(d)
def scale_down(hist, limit, leafkey=lambda s, c: (0, -s), int_key=lambda n: (-1, -n), mode='halve'):
    h = dict(hist)
    while True:
        items = [((c,) + leafkey(s, c), s) for s, c in h.items()]
        d = heap_general2(items, int_key)

        if mode == 'halve': h = {s: max(1, (c + 1) // 2) for s, c in h.items()}
        elif mode == 'halve_floor': h = {s: max(1, c // 2) for s, c in h.items()}

LUMEN brotliDecompressSync -- ERROR CATALOG (black-box, /tmp/orig)
=====================================================================
Vectors: /tmp/agent_b/cases.json, 1021 cases, each {name, hex, orig}. All re-verified against /tmp/orig.
Inputs are at most 1.4 KB. One OK case (out_total_1048576) has a 1 MiB output, so the file is 2.7 MB.
For non-Error throws, "orig" also has "error_type".
Crafting library: /tmp/agent_b/br.py and enc.py. Batch runner: /tmp/agent_b/runner.js (works in orig and node).

Every brotli error is a plain Error with message "brotli: <text>". Its only own property is "message":
there is no stack, code or errno.

1. MESSAGES AND EXACT TRIGGERS (19 brotli messages + 1 runtime RangeError; no others in 120k fuzz cases)
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
"brotli: unexpected end of input"
    Raised by any read that needs a bit beyond the end of the input, at the moment that field or symbol
    is read. Missing bits are never treated as zero.
    - Empty input gives this error.
    - Huffman decoding may look ahead past EOF safely. A 1-bit code that ends exactly at the last input
      bit decodes fine. It fails only if the actual codeword is longer than the bits that remain.
    - Probe: a stream whose remaining literals are all the zero-bit codeword still fails when
      truncated, so there is no zero-fill.
    - Ex: "" ; "0b0180616263" (uncompressed block, then no next header).
"brotli: uncompressed block overruns input"
    ISUNCOMPRESSED=1 and the padding is valid, but MLEN > number of whole bytes left. This is checked
    up front, before any data is copied, including when 0 bytes are left.
    - Ex: "0b0180" ; "5000106162636465".
"brotli: metadata overruns input"
    Metadata block whose padding is valid, but MSKIPLEN > bytes left.
    - Ex: "6b09007879".
"brotli: large-window streams are not supported"
    The 7-bit WBITS pattern 0010001: first bit 1, then 3 bits = 0, then 3 bits = 1.
    - Raised immediately. Following bits do not matter (reserved bit 0 or 1, any 6-bit window), and
      it is raised even if the input ends there.
    - Ex: "11", "91", "11ca".
    - Every other pattern is valid: 16, 17, 18..24, 10..15. There is no other WBITS error.
"brotli: exuberant size nibble"
    MNIBBLES = 5 or 6 and the last (most significant) nibble read is 0.
    - Checked right after the nibbles, before ISUNCOMPRESSED is read; "040000" errors even though the
      input ends there.
    - Applies to uncompressed, compressed and ISLAST blocks.
    - Ex: "2b0000084103".
"brotli: reserved bit set"
    MNIBBLES field = 3 (metadata) and the reserved bit is 1. Checked immediately.
    - Ex: "eb", "eb0003".
"brotli: exuberant metadata size byte"
    MSKIPBYTES >= 2 and the last (most significant) MSKIPLEN byte is 0. Checked right after that byte,
    before padding.
    - Ex: "6b160000".
    - MSKIPBYTES=1 with byte 00 (MSKIPLEN=1) is fine.
"brotli: non-zero padding bits"
    Fill bits up to the byte boundary are not all zero, either after the metadata header (also when
    MSKIPBYTES=0) or after ISUNCOMPRESSED=1.
    - Ex: "20003061626303", "8c03".
    - NOT checked for the final padding after the last meta-block (see section 4).
"brotli: simple code symbol out of range"
    A simple prefix code (HSKIP=1) symbol >= alphabet size. Symbols are ALPHABET_BITS =
    bitlen(alphabet_size-1) bits wide.
    - Checked as each symbol is read, so an invalid first symbol errors even if the input ends right
      after it.
    - Alphabet sizes:
        literal 256 (never triggers)
        insert&copy 704 (704..1023 invalid)
        distance 16+NDIRECT+(48<<NPOSTFIX) (e.g. NDIRECT=1: 65..127 invalid; NPOSTFIX=3,NDIRECT=120: 520+)
        block type NBLTYPES+2
        block count 26 (26..31 invalid)
        context map NTREES+RLEMAX
    - Ex: "1b0300118406" (block-count symbol 26).
"brotli: duplicate simple code symbol"
    Two equal symbols in a simple code.
    - Checked only after all NSYM symbols are read and range-checked. So range wins over a duplicate
      even if the duplicate comes first, and EOF while reading later symbols wins over a duplicate.
    - Checked before the NSYM=4 tree-select bit is read.
    - Ex: "1b010000a0c2c202820004".
"brotli: corrupt code-length code"
    Complex code: the code-length-code lengths (static 2..4-bit code, read in order 1,2,3,4,0,5,17,6,16,
    7..15 starting at index HSKIP) do not form a complete code.
    - Kraft space starts at 32; each length L subtracts 32>>L; reading stops as soon as space == 0.
    - space < 0 errors immediately (no more bits read).
    - Otherwise, after all 18-HSKIP entries, space != 0 errors unless exactly one length is non-zero.
      That covers under-full and all-zero.
    - Exactly one non-zero CL length is accepted: that symbol gets a 0-bit code (e.g. only sym 8 gives
      256 x len-8; only 16 also works).
    - Ex: "1b03000080db01" (1,2,1 over-full), "1b010000800d00000020200800" (2,2 then zeros).
    - HSKIP=2/3 that skips lengths the code needs gives this error too.
"brotli: code-length run overflows alphabet"
    A 16 or 17 repeat (including consecutive-repeat growth) would assign lengths past alphabet_size.
    - A run ending exactly at the alphabet end is OK.
    - This check precedes the space check.
    - Ex: "1b0300000080e3fe1f".
"brotli: prefix code is under/over-subscribed"
    Symbol code lengths are read until the alphabet is full or space (32768) == 0; reading stops at
    space == 0 and the rest are zero.
    - Over-subscription (space < 0) errors immediately. Node instead reads to the alphabet end, so it
      often reports EOF.
    - Errors if the alphabet is exhausted with space > 0. That includes the all-zero code and a complex
      code with a single used symbol.
    - Repeat semantics match RFC/node: 16 repeats the last non-zero length (initially 8). A 0 literal
      does not change it. 17 resets the 16-chain and vice versa.
    - Ex: "1b030000803b01", "1b0300008003e0a2dad405080100".
"brotli: context map run overflows"
    An RLE zero-run (symbol s in 1..RLEMAX) would pass the map end (64*NBLTYPESL or
    4*NBLTYPESD). Checked right after the extra bits.
    - Run length = (1<<s) + an s-bit extra value.
    - Ex: "1b0300008855f000" (RLEMAX=6, run 65 in a 64-entry map).
    - "Context map value out of range" is impossible (symbols are < NTREES+RLEMAX; IMTF keeps values <
      NTREES). The only related error is the simple-code range error.
"brotli: meta-block length mismatch"
    A command produces more than the remaining MLEN.
    (a) Insert overrun: all insert_len literals are decoded first, with no MLEN check during this.
        - Then the error is raised, without reading a distance.
        - So a truncated overrun gives "unexpected end of input" (node gives BLOCK_LENGTH_1 eagerly).
        - Ex: "1b02000020c202850000" (MLEN 3, insert 5).
    (b) Copy overrun: raised after the distance is read and validated.
        - Order: invalid short distance -> dictionary length -> dictionary transform -> MLEN.
        - For dictionary words, the TRANSFORMED length counts. Copy len 8 + OmitLast3 = 5 bytes fits
          MLEN 5.
        - Ex: "1b04000020c202998000", "1b03000020c262909006" (5-byte word, MLEN 4).
    - If the inserts end exactly at MLEN, the meta-block ends: the copy part is ignored and no distance
      is read.
"brotli: invalid short distance"
    Distance codes 4..15 (last+-1..3, second-last+-1..3) give a distance <= 0. Codes 0..3 can never
    fail.
    - Ex: "1b08000020c24a11410a2206" (last=1, code 4).
"brotli: invalid dictionary reference length"
    distance > max_distance, where max_distance = min(total bytes output so far, (1<<WBITS)-16), and
    copy_len is not in 4..24.
    - Includes implicit distance and codes 0..3 at stream start (ring buffer 4,11,15,16 > pos 0).
    - Ex: "1b01000020c202900000" (copy 2, distance 4 at pos 0).
"brotli: invalid dictionary transform"
    Dictionary reference with transform = word_id >> NDBITS[len] >= 121. word_id =
    distance-max_distance-1.
    - Ex: "1b03000020c242906809c8".
"brotli: block length exhausted with a single block type"
    For a category with NBLTYPES=1 the block length is an implicit 2^24 per meta-block. Needing symbol
    2^24+1 of that category in one meta-block raises this.
    - Only reachable via an insert overrun of > 2^24 literals, counted across commands of the
      meta-block. The counter resets per meta-block.
    - Exactly 2^24 literals with MLEN 1 gives "meta-block length mismatch".
    - Ex: "1b00000020c202bf807e4fff01" (vs "...7c4fff01" = 2^24 gives mismatch).
RangeError "Invalid typed array length"  (not a brotli message)
    Decode succeeded but output > 1,048,576 bytes. This is the runtime's 1 MiB cap on any
    TypedArray/Buffer; fs.readFileSync of > 1 MiB fails the same way.
    - The decoder itself is not limited: a brotli error found after > 1 MiB of output still wins.
    - Exactly 1 MiB is OK.
    - Ex: "9f0000100020c2e2b18074ef1f00" (1 MiB + 1). Valid 6-nibble meta-blocks always hit this.

2. PARSE ORDER (first failing check wins; everything is sequential, deferred checks as noted)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Stream header:
  WBITS (marker -> large-window error).
Meta-block header, loop:
  ISLAST; [ISLASTEMPTY -> stream ends]; MNIBBLES.
  Metadata branch:
    reserved -> MSKIPBYTES -> bytes -> exuberant byte -> padding -> overrun -> skip.
    If ISLAST, end.
  Data branch:
    nibbles -> exuberant -> [ISUNCOMPRESSED if !ISLAST].
    Uncompressed: padding -> overrun -> copy.
Compressed header (RFC order):
  NBLTYPES/btype code/bcount code/first count for L, I, D -> NPOSTFIX, NDIRECT -> cmodes ->
  NTREESL + cmap -> NTREESD + cmap -> literal, command and distance codes.
Commands until remaining <= 0:
  [I switch] -> cmd symbol + insert/copy extra -> literals (each with [L switch]) ->
  [insert MLEN check] -> [stop if done] -> distance (implicit, or [D switch] + symbol + extra) ->
  short-distance check -> dict(len, transform) or copy -> MLEN check.
Semantics all confirmed equal to node on valid data:
  - Window rule max_distance = min(pos, 2^WBITS-16) holds (WBITS=10: d=1008 copies, d=1009 is a
    dictionary word).
  - Dictionary refs and code 0 do not update the distance ring buffer.
  - Block-type ring buffer starts at (1,0); sym0 = second-to-last, sym1 = last+1 mod N, else sym-2.
  - All 26 block-count codes.
  - NBLTYPES 1..256 (varlen8 caps at 256; >256 is not encodable).
  - NTREES up to 256; RLEMAX 1..16 and IMTF.
  - Context modes 0..3 (MSB6 too, which node never emits).
  - NPOSTFIX 0..3 and NDIRECT up to 120.
  - Zero-length transformed words are accepted.

3. EOF / TRUNCATION SUMMARY
--------------------------
Node streams q5/q11 (one meta-block, 344..7059 B) and flush-built 5-meta-block streams (490/497 B,
including an uncompressed block) were cut at every length.
- Every prefix gives "unexpected end of input".
- Exception: prefixes that end inside an uncompressed block's payload, with the header complete
  and 0..MLEN-1 payload bytes present, give "uncompressed block overruns input". Full length gives OK.
- 29k prefixes of 250 crafted valid vectors gave only those two messages, plus "metadata overruns
  input" inside metadata payloads. OK only appeared when nothing but trailing garbage was removed.

4. LAX BEHAVIOURS / DIFFERENCES FROM NODE
----------------------------------------
- Final padding is NOT checked (node: ERR__ERROR_FORMAT_PADDING_2). This covers the bits after
  ISLAST+ISLASTEMPTY and after a compressed ISLAST block.
  - "deadbeef" -> OK empty. Also "fb" -> OK, "81ff" -> OK.
  - Example "1b040000a0cbd0d8de040a01488d" -> "hello".
- Trailing bytes after the stream end are ignored (node too).
- Otherwise exactly as strict as node: in 100k differential mutated streams there was no
  orig-OK/node-fail except PADDING_2, no orig-fail/node-OK, and no differing output.
- Message mapping to node codes:
  - CL_SPACE -> corrupt code-length code
  - HUFFMAN_SPACE -> under/over-subscribed, or run overflows alphabet for repeat overflow
  - BLOCK_LENGTH_1/2 -> meta-block length mismatch (or EOF, since literals are read first)
  - DISTANCE -> invalid short distance
  - DICTIONARY -> invalid dictionary reference length
  - TRANSFORM -> invalid dictionary transform
  - CONTEXT_MAP_REPEAT -> context map run overflows
  - PADDING_1 -> non-zero padding bits
  - RESERVED -> reserved bit set
  - EXUBERANT_NIBBLE / EXUBERANT_META_NIBBLE -> exuberant size nibble / metadata size byte
  - SIMPLE_HUFFMAN_ALPHABET / SAME -> out of range / duplicate
  - WINDOW_BITS -> large-window
  - Z_BUF_ERROR -> unexpected end of input, or the two overrun messages
- Order differences from node:
  - Insert overrun: node fails before reading literals.
  - Over-subscribed code: orig fails at once, node reads on (often EOF).

5. VALID-STREAM CONFORMANCE
--------------------------
Every set matched byte-for-byte:
- 1880 node streams: q0..11, lgwin 10..24, modes 0..2, 12 inputs (0 B..40 KB).
- 69 large node streams up to 1 MiB output: LGBLOCK, NPOSTFIX/NDIRECT, disabled literal context modeling.
- 3150 random crafted valid streams: all header features, dictionary refs with all transforms,
  windows 10..24, mixed metadata/uncompressed/compressed blocks.
- An exhaustive set: 121 transforms x lengths 4..24 x 3 words.

6. INPUT ARG (side note)
------------------------
- Input is converted like Buffer.from: strings as UTF-8; arrays and ArrayBuffer are accepted.
- A DataView decodes as empty input (gives "unexpected end of input").
- Number, null or undefined -> TypeError "Buffer.from: unsupported value".

content.text:
I've built the compression module in `/workspace/src/compress/`. All five encoders reproduce the original byte-for-byte, and all decoders match its outputs and exact error messages on every case I tested. It compiles warning-free under the workspace's own `Cargo.toml` (std only, no `unsafe`, edition 2021), and its 12 unit tests pass in release and debug builds. I never built in `/workspace` and never ran `compile.sh`; checks ran on a copy under `/tmp`.

**Files:** `mod.rs` (API plus the documentation you'll implement the JS side from), `checksum.rs`, `inflate.rs`, `deflate.rs`, `brotli_dec.rs`, `brotli_enc.rs`, `brotli_dict.bin`, `zstd_dec.rs`, `zstd_enc.rs`. I got the brotli dictionary by decoding crafted streams with node's decoder; its SHA-256 matches the published RFC value.

**API:** your spec's functions (`crc32`, `adler32`, deflate/zlib/gzip encode and decode, `unzip_decode`, brotli and zstd), plus:
- **`Codec`:** maps each stream class and each `CompressionStream` format to its codec.
- **`BufferedCodec`:** buffers written chunks and runs the codec once at the end.
- **`ZLIB_CONSTANTS`:** `zlib.constants` with the original's 170 keys, order and values.
- **`CodecError`:** `message` is the original's exact text. The original's errors have no `code` or `errno`, so `code` is always `""` and `errno` always `0`; don't expose them to JS.

**How I checked it**
- **Encoders:** 825 outputs across all formats (empty to ~1 MB, text, random, runs, matches farther than 32 KB), plus about 980 extra brotli cases. All identical.
- **Decoders:** over 30,000 crafted, fuzzed and valid inputs (node, libzstd, Python zlib), compared directly against the original. All identical, including all 40 bundled assets.

**What you need to know for the bindings** (full detail with sample outputs is in the `mod.rs` doc comment):
- **Options are never read.** That covers level, strategy, windowBits, `dictionary`, `info`, `maxOutputLength`, `chunkSize` and all brotli/zstd params. Nothing is validated and nothing throws for bad options.
- **The original is lax in specific ways:**
  - **zlib wrapper:** neither Adler-32 nor FCHECK is checked.
  - **gzip:** CRC and length are not checked. Only the first member is decoded and trailing garbage is ignored.
  - **unzip:** `unzipSync` is just gunzip, with no zlib auto-detection.
  - **brotli:** large-window streams are rejected.
  - **zstd:** checksums are verified and trailing bytes are an error.
- **The compressors are weak:**
  - **deflate:** one fixed-Huffman block with greedy matching. Matches farther than 32 KB produce corrupt streams; I reproduce that deliberately.
  - **brotli:** literal-only, or stored.
  - **zstd:** raw and RLE blocks only.
- **Async functions** (`zlib.gzip(buf, cb)` etc.) run the job in a single microtask and never throw synchronously.
- **Streams and Compression/DecompressionStream** buffer all input and emit exactly one output chunk at `end()`/`close()`. The exact JS class model, event order and error behaviour are in the doc comment.
- **1 MiB cap:** the original's engine refuses any typed array over 1 MiB (`RangeError: Invalid typed array length`). That caps every result; this module has no such limit.

**Known differences and untestable areas**
- **`dictionary` argument:** on `inflate_raw`/`zlib_decode` it is an extension the original doesn't have; pass `None` to match it.
- **Inputs above 1 MiB:** these can't be compared against the original. Brotli inputs over 16 MiB are split into several meta-blocks (node decodes them correctly), and the zstd 8-byte content-size field is written per spec.
- **Decompression bombs:** there is no output cap, so a malicious input can make the decoders allocate very large outputs.

I used four subagents for the JS-API, stream and decoder-error investigations, then spot-checked their key claims myself. One of them once printed `zlib.Gunzip` with `console.log`, which showed the class source. It disclosed this and re-confirmed every related claim with black-box tests, and I didn't use that output.

Scratch work is all under `/tmp`: `compress_dev`, `compress_final`, `ws_check`, `x`, `agent_*`.
